newsitem.title: MACEDONIA: OPPOSITION CHARGES FRAUD IN MACEDONIA VOTE.
newsitem.headline: OPPOSITION CHARGES FRAUD IN MACEDONIA VOTE.

text.p: Macedonians voted on Sunday in hotly-contested local elections as opposition parties alleged widespread fraud.
First results of an election widely seen as a referendum on the ruling Social Democrats' rapid free-market reforms are expected on Monday.
It was the first local ballot under the country's new council system established after Macedonia split away from the former Yugoslav Federation in 1991.
The Social Democrats insisted voting went off smoothly with only a few minor problems, unlikely to alter the outcome.
But a spokesman for the main opposition party VMRO-DPME, Dragi Ivanovski, alleged authorities were trying to rig the vote.
"(The Social Democrats) are trying to have a very small turnout so that the system of fraud can start functioning," Ivanovski said.
Many people were unable to vote because their names had been removed from electoral lists and in one district in the capital, three entire streets had "disappeared," the spokesman added.

An observer mission from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe said it was still too early to comment on complaints and said they would issue a definitive statement by Tuesday morning at the earliest.
In the predominantly Albanian town of Tetovo, frustrated would-be voters gathered in clutches outside polling stations.
"My name was on the list when I checked last week," said one angry man who asked not to be named. "But now it's gone. The strange thing is that my wife's name is there."
A candidate for the right-wing Democratic Party for Macedonia in Tetovo, Zoran Efremov, said his name was not on the list but his wife and parents who live in the same house were.
Opposition parties said they feared the Social Democrats would top up the ballot boxes with votes in their favour, and then declare a good turnout.
Social Democrat spokesman Nake Stojanovski rejected the allegations and told Reuters that by late Sunday afternoon, the elections had gone well.
"So far our information is that the voting has been well organised and the response has been quite good," he said.
One opposition party had violated the election rules by running political advertising on Sunday, and others were handing out leaflets outside polling booths, he added.
But he said there were "no serious problems".
Analysts predicted parties representing the country's large ethnic Albanian minority would emerge stronger.
In the Albanian-dominated western districts, the Albanian parties could win up to 40 town councils, handing them a power base that mainstream parties would find hard to ignore.
Opposition parliament member Naum Simjanovski of the Liberal Party said the vote would force the government of Prime Minister Branko Crvenkovski to address issues raised by the opposition.
The opposition VMRO-DPME has called the ruling party's privatisation programme "unjust" and has urged a more cautious approach to economic reform.
